clue.text: Might train crash? Without a doubt!

parts.note: might means force or power

indicators.note: a train crash leaves the carriages jumbled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wondering whether a train could crash, and answering emphatically that it could.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might' looks like a verb asking a question, but it is a noun meaning strength; 'crash' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean surely, beyond any question.

clue.text: Fingered the material

explanation.surface: Someone running their hand over some fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Felt is the past tense of feel, to touch, and also a matted woollen fabric.

clue.text: Hooligans stamp into banks

indicators.note: into says the stamp goes inside the word for banks

parts.note: banks are rows, as in banks of seats or keys
a die is a tool that stamps a design onto metal

explanation.surface: Thugs storming into banks.
explanation.definitionFit: Rowdies are noisy, rough troublemakers.

clue.text: Withdraw missile finally in agreement over weapons

indicators.note: in a down entry over means the earlier pieces sit above the weapons
finally points to the closing letter of the word missile

parts.note: people in agreement are at one
swords are weapons

explanation.surface: Arms negotiators agree to pull back a missile.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat one's words is to retract what one has said.

clue.text: Englishmen put up in temporary accommodation, an apartment

indicators.note: in says the reversed men go inside the shelter

parts.note: a tent is shelter for a short stay

indicators.note: in a down entry put up means written upwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: E for English followed by men

explanation.surface: English people housed in a temporary shelter, which is a flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' reverses the letters of Englishmen read as E plus MEN; in Scotland 'tenement' names a flat, not only the building.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland a tenement is a flat within a large shared building.

clue.text: Hard water? It depends

parts.note: water frozen hard and dangling, depending in the old sense of hanging down

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard water' looks like limescale chemistry and 'It depends' like an evasion; it is frozen water that hangs.
explanation.definitionFit: An icicle is a hanging spike of ice.

clue.text: Go and sing

explanation.surface: An invitation to leave and to burst into song.
explanation.definitionFit: Scat! is a curt order to go away, and to scat is to sing jazz in nonsense syllables.

clue.text: Use this in a game, we hear, and triumph

indicators.note: we hear says the answer is said like the name of the chestnut

parts.note: a conker is a horse chestnut on a string used in the British children's game of conkers

explanation.surface: A tip that using this in a game will bring victory.
explanation.walkthrough: In conkers, a British playground game, children swing chestnuts on strings at each other's.
explanation.definitionFit: To conquer is to win, overcome or prevail.

clue.text: Cheap sort of opera

explanation.surface: A low-budget kind of opera production.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worth threepence, an old British coin, is worthless; The Threepenny Opera is Brecht and Weill's work.

clue.text: It's not the real game

parts.note: real tennis is the original indoor court game, so the outdoor version on grass is the one that is not real tennis

explanation.walkthrough: Real tennis is the old indoor game played in walled courts; the everyday game played outside is its younger offshoot.
explanation.definitionFit: The modern outdoor racket sport is distinguished from real, or royal, tennis.

clue.text: Not, so to speak, the back line

indicators.note: back means the word for the line is read from its end to its start

parts.note: a rank is a line of soldiers standing side by side

explanation.surface: A remark that the rear row is not, as it were, really a line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not, so to speak' asks for a word said like 'not', namely a knot; a knar is a knot in wood.
explanation.definitionFit: A knar is a gnarled lump in a tree trunk, which sounds like the spoken word not.

clue.text: Old fogy not quite ready to transport fish

indicators.note: not quite means the word for ready loses its final letter

parts.note: fruit that is ripe is ready to eat
a van is a vehicle for transport
a winkle is a small edible shellfish, loosely a fish

explanation.surface: An elderly bore who is not quite ready to carry fish.
explanation.walkthrough: In Washington Irving's tale Rip Van Winkle sleeps twenty years and wakes out of date.
explanation.definitionFit: The name stands for someone hopelessly behind the times.

clue.text: With people around, I look

indicators.note: around says the people stand about the single letter, enclosing it

parts.note: people here means men, as in a body of workers

explanation.surface: Someone surrounded by a crowd, glancing about.
explanation.definitionFit: Mien is a person's bearing or appearance, the way they look.

clue.text: Foreign character has some scope — not a lot

parts.note: mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet, a foreign character

indicators.note: not means the following small word is dropped from the scope word

parts.note: to have some latitude is to have some scope or freedom
taken as written

explanation.surface: A foreigner who is allowed only a little freedom of action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not a lot' looks like one phrase meaning little; 'not a' removes A from LATITUDE and 'lot' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A multitude is a great number, a large quantity.

clue.text: Bureaucratic plan is more complicated

indicators.note: complicated means tangled up, so these letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A scheme that is overly complex, as officialdom's tend to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'more' looks like part of 'more complicated', but it is fodder; only 'complicated' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Bureaucracy is cold and faceless, treating people without warmth.

clue.text: Applying to the wrong purpose lost uranium that's concealed

indicators.note: concealed means the element is kept inside the word for lost

parts.note: something lost is missing
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: Uranium that went missing after being hidden, then put to an evil use.
explanation.definitionFit: To misuse something is to employ it for an improper end.

clue.text: Opposed to a bit of the Bible

parts.note: a verse is one numbered portion of a Bible chapter

explanation.surface: Someone who objects to a passage of scripture.
explanation.definitionFit: Being averse to something means disliking or resisting it.

clue.text: Hungry? Here's tart and cake

parts.note: tart means sharp in taste
to cake is to set hard

explanation.surface: An offer of tart and cake to someone who is peckish.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharp-set is an old term for keenly hungry.

clue.text: Game's ending rejected by inventor

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the call is read in reverse

parts.note: no side is the referee's call ending a rugby match

explanation.surface: An inventor who refuses to accept how a match finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No side' is the old rugby term for the final whistle; it reads backwards as the name of the American inventor of the light bulb and phonograph.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Edison was a prolific American inventor.

clue.text: Picture shows one West End star holding a drink

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: holding means the star's name encloses the drink

parts.note: Mae West was a film star, the star whose name ends in West
gin is a drink

explanation.surface: A photograph of a London theatre star holding a glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West End' suggests London theatreland; it is the star whose surname, at the end, is West.
explanation.definitionFit: To picture something is to form a mental image of it.

clue.text: Double feature evokes cheers

indicators.note: double means the feature word is written twice in a row

parts.note: the chin is a facial feature

explanation.surface: A double-bill film that brings applause from the audience.
explanation.definitionFit: Chin-chin is an old-fashioned toast, said when raising a glass.

clue.text: A heart I break, as a mistress

indicators.note: break means smash, so these letters are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A woman confesses to breaking a heart as someone's lover.
explanation.definitionFit: A hetaira was a courtesan in ancient Greece.

clue.text: Sylphs very easily look thus, especially their faces

definitions.text: Sylphs very easily look thus, especially their faces

indicators.note: their faces means the front letter of each of these words

explanation.surface: Slender spirits look elegantly slim, above all in the face.
explanation.definitionFit: Svelte means slender and graceful, which is how sylphs appear.

clue.text: Watch put back

explanation.surface: A watch that has been set back an hour.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand over someone is to supervise them closely, and to stand something over is to postpone it.

clue.text: Nine letters returned? Just one, from overseas

indicators.note: returned means the phrase for the nine letters is read backwards

parts.note: the first nine letters of the alphabet run from A to I

explanation.surface: A question about how many of nine letters came back, with the answer: only one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from overseas' marks the definition as Greek: the smallest Greek letter, used for a tiny amount.
explanation.definitionFit: An iota is a Greek letter and, by extension, a minute quantity, the merest jot.

clue.text: Food for grouse

explanation.surface: Something eaten by a game bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef is meat from cattle, and to beef is to complain.

clue.text: 2¼" banana, ill-favoured in part

indicators.note: in part says the answer is a portion of the words banana and ill-favoured run together

explanation.surface: A small, unattractive banana of a couple of inches.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the measurement itself: 2¼ inches is an old cloth measure.
explanation.definitionFit: A nail was an old English unit of length for cloth, equal to two and a quarter inches.

clue.text: Pickles fan gets roughed up by this weapon

indicators.note: roughed up means knocked about, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A supporter of someone called Pickles gets beaten up by an assailant.
explanation.definitionFit: A clasp-knife is a folding knife, which can be carried as a weapon.

clue.text: Look and sound like a king

indicators.note: sound like says the answer is pronounced the same as the king's name

parts.note: Lear is the king in Shakespeare's tragedy

explanation.surface: Advice to look and speak like a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: To leer is to give a sly or lecherous look.

clue.text: The crafty French let a man on the pitch

indicators.note: crafty means artful or devious, so the letters are cunningly rearranged

explanation.surface: The French, being cunning, allow a player onto the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The crafty French' looks like a phrase about the French people; THE is a link and FRENCH LET A is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A centre-half is a player in the middle of a football defence.
